items.prompt: What does the strangler fig pattern actually replace a big-bang rewrite with?
choices: A faster rewrite of the exact same system, done in roughly half the time
A routing facade that sends traffic to old or new system per route, migrated incrementally with both systems live
A tool that fully automates rewriting legacy code into brand-new code
A freeze on shipping any new features until the whole rewrite finishes
items.explanation: The pattern's core mechanism is a facade deciding, per route, which system answers — allowing migration one capability at a time instead of one all-or-nothing cutover, with both systems running simultaneously the whole time.
items.reflection: The strangler fig pattern is really an instance of a bigger idea: replace a thing by growing a new one around it while the old one keeps functioning, instead of stopping the world to swap it out. Where else, inside or outside software, have you seen an old thing kept deliberately alive while a new one grows up around it, rather than being torn out first?

items.prompt: A team says they are doing a strangler fig migration, but their plan is: build the whole new system in a branch, then swap it in on one deploy. Is that actually the strangler fig pattern?
choices: Yes — any eventual replacement of the old system counts as this pattern
No — the defining feature is incremental migration behind a facade with both systems live, not a single swap regardless of how the new system was built
Yes, as long as the resulting new system is objectively better code
No — it only counts as this pattern if the migration takes over a year
items.explanation: A single swap, even of a well-built replacement, is a big-bang cutover in disguise — it carries the same all-or-nothing risk the pattern exists to avoid. The name applies specifically to gradual, facade-mediated migration.
items.reflection: The strangler fig pattern is really an instance of a bigger idea: replace a thing by growing a new one around it while the old one keeps functioning, instead of stopping the world to swap it out. Where else, inside or outside software, have you seen an old thing kept deliberately alive while a new one grows up around it, rather than being torn out first?

items.prompt: Why is the plant metaphor (strangler fig) actually apt for this pattern, beyond just being a memorable name?
choices: It is not actually apt at all, in any meaningful technical sense — it is purely a catchy marketing name
The fig grows to full independence around the host while the host stays alive, and only afterward does the host get removed — matching new-system-grows-around-old-while-both-run, retire-old-last
It is apt mainly because real strangler figs happen to grow noticeably faster than most other plants
It is apt because the fig and its host tree are technically classified as the same biological species
items.explanation: The biological process is a precise structural match: the fig never requires the host to stop functioning while it grows, and removal of the host happens only after the fig is already self-sufficient — exactly the sequencing a good migration follows.
items.reflection: The strangler fig pattern is really an instance of a bigger idea: replace a thing by growing a new one around it while the old one keeps functioning, instead of stopping the world to swap it out. Where else, inside or outside software, have you seen an old thing kept deliberately alive while a new one grows up around it, rather than being torn out first?

items.prompt: In a strangler fig migration, which system actually answers a given client request?
choices: Whichever one the facade decides, old or new, per route
Always the new system, immediately
Always the legacy system, until the whole migration is complete
The client's own code decides directly, without a facade
items.explanation: The facade is what makes the per-route decision. Neither backend nor the client decides this on its own.

items.prompt: Does the strangler fig pattern require freezing the legacy system's feature work while the migration runs?
choices: No — both systems can keep evolving while the migration proceeds
Yes, the legacy system must be fully frozen the entire time
Yes, but only for the first month of the migration
Only if the new system is smaller than the old one
items.explanation: A feature freeze belongs to the big-bang approach this pattern exists to avoid, not to the pattern itself.

items.prompt: What unit of work gets migrated one at a time in a strangler fig migration?
choices: A route or capability
A single source file, regardless of what it does
The entire system, all at once
A single developer's laptop setup
items.explanation: Migration happens at the level of a route, endpoint, page, or workflow — a unit small enough to reason about and roll back independently.

items.prompt: When does the legacy code behind an already-migrated route actually get deleted?
choices: Only later, as a deliberate retirement step once the new path has proven itself
Immediately, the moment the route's traffic moves to the new system
It never gets deleted under this pattern
Automatically, as soon as the facade is deployed
items.explanation: Migrated and retired are different states — the legacy path survives as a rollback target until a separate, deliberate decision removes it.

items.prompt: What does the real strangler fig plant do to its host tree while it is still growing?
choices: Grows around it while the host stays alive and functioning
Kills the host tree instantly on contact
Has no relationship to the host tree at all
Replaces the host's root system within days
items.explanation: The host keeps living and functioning for years while the fig matures — that coexistence is exactly the property the software pattern borrows.

items.prompt: Which best describes the overall shape of a strangler fig migration?
choices: Gradual, facade-mediated, both systems live the whole time
A single cutover event planned months in advance
A sequence of complete, independent rewrites run in parallel by separate teams
An automated tool that translates legacy code line by line
items.explanation: The shape is defined by gradualness and a mediating facade, not by automation or a scheduled single event.

items.prompt: What is the facade's job in a strangler fig migration?
choices: Automatically rewriting legacy logic into a cleaner, modern coding style
Deciding, per request, whether the legacy or new system answers — invisibly to the client
Storing every piece of application data for the duration of the migration
Running the legacy system's automated test suite on a fixed schedule
items.explanation: The facade is a thin routing layer, not a logic-rewriting tool or a data store. Its only job is deciding which backend answers a given request, in a way the client never has to know about.
items.reflection: The facade's job here is really 'centralize a decision instead of scattering it' — the same principle shows up any time a system needs one source of truth for a choice that otherwise gets duplicated inconsistently, like a feature-flag service or a DNS record. Where have you seen a decision scattered across many places that really belonged in one?

items.prompt: A developer adds an if/else check for which system to call directly inside the client's checkout page component. Is that equivalent to a strangler fig facade?
choices: Yes — it has the same effect as a facade, just placed in a different location
No — it scatters the routing decision into client code instead of centralizing it in one facade, making it harder to change or roll back consistently
Yes, as long as the flag controlling it is stored in a config file somewhere
No, but only because client code is technically unable to call two systems
items.explanation: Centralizing the decision in one facade is what makes flipping a route, or rolling one back, a single, consistent, testable change. Scattering the same check across client code means every scattered copy has to be found and flipped in sync.
items.reflection: The facade's job here is really 'centralize a decision instead of scattering it' — the same principle shows up any time a system needs one source of truth for a choice that otherwise gets duplicated inconsistently, like a feature-flag service or a DNS record. Where have you seen a decision scattered across many places that really belonged in one?

items.prompt: A team builds its facade's routing decision as a single environment variable, read once when the process starts, that cannot be changed without a redeploy. Is that a workable strangler fig facade?
choices: No — the whole point is routing decisions changeable per route without a redeploy; baking it into a startup-only variable reintroduces the big-bang rollback problem
Yes, environment variables are always an equally good choice
Yes, as long as the variable is well documented
No, but only because environment variables are inherently insecure
items.explanation: A routing decision that needs a redeploy to change loses the entire advantage of per-route rollback in seconds — it is functionally closer to a big-bang cutover than a strangler fig facade.
items.reflection: The facade's job here is really 'centralize a decision instead of scattering it' — the same principle shows up any time a system needs one source of truth for a choice that otherwise gets duplicated inconsistently, like a feature-flag service or a DNS record. Where have you seen a decision scattered across many places that really belonged in one?

items.prompt: Two separately deployed facade instances each keep their own independent copy of the routing table for the same routes, with no shared source of truth between them. What is the risk?
choices: The two tables can drift out of sync, so the same route may be served by different systems depending on which instance handled a given request
No risk at all — facades are stateless, so this is always fine
The legacy system will immediately crash
This is actually the recommended way to run a facade
items.explanation: The facade's value depends on the routing decision being one coherent source of truth. Letting two independent copies drift reintroduces exactly the inconsistency the pattern is meant to eliminate.
items.reflection: The facade's job here is really 'centralize a decision instead of scattering it' — the same principle shows up any time a system needs one source of truth for a choice that otherwise gets duplicated inconsistently, like a feature-flag service or a DNS record. Where have you seen a decision scattered across many places that really belonged in one?

items.prompt: Does the client need to know which backend system actually served its request?
choices: No — that is the whole point of putting the decision behind a facade
Yes, the client must inspect a response header on every request
Yes, the client chooses the backend itself
Only for write requests, never for reads
items.explanation: The facade's decision is meant to be invisible to the client — that invisibility is what lets the decision change without touching client code.

items.prompt: Is the facade responsible for rewriting the legacy system's business logic?
choices: No — its only job is routing, not rewriting logic
Yes, it gradually rewrites legacy logic in place
Yes, but only for read-only routes
It replaces the legacy system's database schema
items.explanation: The facade is a routing layer. Rewriting logic happens in the new system being built behind it, not inside the facade itself.

items.prompt: Where does the routing decision live in a well-built strangler fig setup?
choices: Centrally, in the facade
Duplicated in every client
Inside the legacy system's own source code
Nowhere — it is decided randomly each time
items.explanation: Centralizing the decision in the facade is what makes it a single, consistent, easily reversible change.

items.prompt: A route has not been explicitly configured in the routing table yet. Which system should it fall back to by default?
choices: Legacy — safe by default
New — new is always assumed safe
Whichever system responded fastest last time
No system — the request should simply fail
items.explanation: Defaulting an unconfigured route to legacy means nothing can accidentally land on unproven new code just because nobody set it up yet.

items.prompt: Which existing piece of infrastructure is the facade's role most similar to?
choices: A reverse proxy that decides which backend handles a request by rule
A database replication process
A CSS bundler
A DNS registrar
items.explanation: Like a reverse proxy, the facade sits in front of backends and decides, per request, where traffic goes — just based on migration state rather than raw load.

items.prompt: What is the minimum change needed to migrate a single route once the facade exists?
choices: Flipping that route's entry in the facade's routing table
Redeploying the legacy system
Rewriting the client application
Changing the DNS record for the whole domain
items.explanation: Because the facade centralizes the decision, migrating a route is a small, targeted change to its table entry — nothing else needs to move.

items.prompt: What is the core risk a big-bang rewrite carries that a strangler fig migration avoids?
choices: Big-bang rewrites are, as a near-universal rule, always written in a strictly worse programming language
All the value is delivered at once, on one cutover, made by people who may not remember every rule the old system encodes — with no small, reversible steps along the way
Big-bang rewrites are, by their very nature, fundamentally incompatible with using version control at all
There is no real difference in risk between the two approaches whatsoever, once you account for team size
items.explanation: A single cutover concentrates all the risk into one event, with no intermediate checkpoints and no way to isolate a failure to a small piece. A strangler fig migration spreads the same total risk across many small, independently reversible steps.
items.reflection: The real contrast here is not big-bang versus gradual as a software-specific idea — it is one large irreversible bet versus many small reversible ones, a trade-off that shows up anywhere a plan touches something real people depend on. Where have you seen a team choose a single big bet when a sequence of small, reversible ones was actually available?

items.prompt: A big-bang rewrite that ships successfully on its first attempt still has one structural downside compared to a strangler fig migration that took the same total calendar time. What is it?
choices: It has none at all — a rewrite that ships successfully is strictly better
Customers saw zero improvement for the entire duration, and the team had no real production feedback until the very end
It always costs more money overall, regardless of how the outcome turns out
It can't realistically be tested at all before the moment it finally ships
items.explanation: Even a rewrite that eventually succeeds still delayed all value delivery to the final cutover and got no real production signal on any of its assumptions until then — a strangler fig migration gets both value and feedback continuously, which is a structural advantage independent of whether the rewrite worked.
items.reflection: The real contrast here is not big-bang versus gradual as a software-specific idea — it is one large irreversible bet versus many small reversible ones, a trade-off that shows up anywhere a plan touches something real people depend on. Where have you seen a team choose a single big bet when a sequence of small, reversible ones was actually available?

items.prompt: If migrating one route behind a facade exposes a bug in the new system, what is the rollback compared to a big-bang rewrite's rollback?
choices: Both approaches require roughly the same total amount of rollback effort and calendar time either way
The facade migration only needs that one route flipped back; the big-bang rewrite has no equivalent small move — the only rollback is reverting the entire cutover
Neither approach can realistically be rolled back once it has already shipped to production traffic
The big-bang rewrite is actually easier to roll back, since it is packaged as one single atomic deploy
items.explanation: Per-route rollback in a facade migration is a single, small, targeted change. A big-bang rewrite has no unit smaller than the whole cutover to roll back — a bug found anywhere forces reverting everything, usually under time pressure.
items.reflection: The real contrast here is not big-bang versus gradual as a software-specific idea — it is one large irreversible bet versus many small reversible ones, a trade-off that shows up anywhere a plan touches something real people depend on. Where have you seen a team choose a single big bet when a sequence of small, reversible ones was actually available?

items.prompt: When does a big-bang rewrite typically deliver its first improvement to actual customers?
choices: At the final cutover, whenever that happens
Every week, incrementally, like a strangler fig migration
On day one of the project
Improvements are delivered continuously throughout, same as a gradual migration
items.explanation: A big-bang rewrite withholds all value until the single cutover event — that is exactly the structural downside the pattern is designed around.

items.prompt: In a strangler fig migration, how large is the unit of rollback if one migrated route turns out buggy?
choices: Just that one route
The entire system
Every route migrated that calendar month
There is no way to roll back at all
items.explanation: Per-route rollback is the direct payoff of routing per route instead of per deploy.

items.prompt: What is the main structural reason a big-bang rewrite is considered risky, independent of the team's skill?
choices: It bets the entire investment on a single cutover event with no intermediate checkpoints
Rewrites are always written using buggier tools than migrations
Rewrites cannot be reviewed by a second engineer
Rewrites take longer than any other kind of software project by definition
items.explanation: The risk is structural, about how the bet is placed, not about skill or tooling.

items.prompt: A strangler fig migration and a big-bang rewrite can both end up at the exact same final system. What differs between them?
choices: How risk is distributed on the way there
Nothing meaningful differs once they reach the same end state
Only the programming language used
Only the number of engineers assigned
items.explanation: Same destination, very different risk profile along the way — that is the entire basis for preferring one approach over the other.

items.prompt: Why does a strangler fig migration get real production feedback earlier than a big-bang rewrite?
choices: Because each migrated route is exposed to real traffic as soon as it ships, not just at a final cutover
Because it uses more automated tests than a rewrite
Because it is always built by a larger team
Because the legacy system is deleted immediately
items.explanation: Shipping piece by piece means each piece meets real traffic right away, instead of all pieces meeting real traffic for the first time on cutover night.

items.prompt: If a strangler fig migration stalls halfway through, what is true of the routes already migrated?
choices: They remain live and working on the new system regardless of the stall
They automatically revert to legacy the moment the project stalls
They become permanently broken
They must be migrated again from scratch
items.explanation: Each migrated route stands on its own — a stalled migration simply leaves some routes on legacy and some on new, rather than losing everything shipped so far.

items.prompt: What is the facade's core data structure, and what does flipping one entry in it actually do?
choices: A cache of legacy responses — flipping an entry just clears that cache
A lookup table mapping route to target system — flipping an entry is the entire mechanism of migrating that route, with no client change or redeploy needed
A queue of pending migrations that gets processed one route per day
A direct copy of the legacy system's source code, edited in place by hand
items.explanation: The routing table is deliberately the single source of truth for who owns this traffic right now. Changing one entry is a config-level change, not a code change — no client update, no DNS change, no legacy redeploy required.
items.reflection: A small lookup table as the single source of truth for a decision is a pattern that shows up well beyond routing — feature flags, A/B test assignment, and permission checks all lean on the same idea: one table, flipped in place, instead of logic scattered through the codebase. Where else have you seen one small table carry an outsized amount of a system's behavior?

items.prompt: `GET /products` is flagged new and `POST /orders` is flagged legacy in the routing table at the same moment. Is that a valid state?
choices: No — all routes must migrate together or the overall system is inconsistent
Yes — different routes can be served by different systems simultaneously; that is the entire point of routing per route instead of per deploy
No — the facade can only ever forward traffic to one backend at a time
Yes, but only when both routes happen to share the same HTTP method
items.explanation: Per-route routing is exactly what lets a low-risk route (read-only catalog) run on the new system while a high-risk route (order writes) stays on legacy until it has earned that move separately.
items.reflection: A small lookup table as the single source of truth for a decision is a pattern that shows up well beyond routing — feature flags, A/B test assignment, and permission checks all lean on the same idea: one table, flipped in place, instead of logic scattered through the codebase. Where else have you seen one small table carry an outsized amount of a system's behavior?

items.prompt: At 2am, a route flagged new turns out to have a bug. What is the actual incident response?
choices: Redeploy the legacy system from scratch to take back that traffic
Flip that one routing table entry back to legacy — a config change to one line, not a code revert or redeploy
Roll back every already-migrated route in the system, not just this one
Take the entire site offline for everyone until a real fix can ship
items.explanation: Because routing decisions live in one small table, the incident response is scoped to exactly the affected route: flip its entry back. Nothing else changes, and no deploy of either backend is required.
items.reflection: A small lookup table as the single source of truth for a decision is a pattern that shows up well beyond routing — feature flags, A/B test assignment, and permission checks all lean on the same idea: one table, flipped in place, instead of logic scattered through the codebase. Where else have you seen one small table carry an outsized amount of a system's behavior?

items.prompt: What does a route's entry in the routing table actually record?
choices: Which system currently owns that route's traffic
The total number of requests that route has ever received
A copy of the route's legacy source code
The date the route was originally created
items.explanation: The table's only job is recording the current target for each route, nothing more.

items.prompt: Does changing a routing table entry require redeploying the legacy system?
choices: No — it is a config-level change
Yes, every time
Only on weekends
Only if more than ten routes change at once
items.explanation: Flipping an entry is deliberately decoupled from deploying either backend.

items.prompt: Can two different routes point at two different systems at the same time?
choices: Yes — that is the entire point of per-route routing
No — every route must point at the same system at once
Only if they share the same HTTP method
Only during a maintenance window
items.explanation: Per-route routing is what lets low-risk and high-risk routes migrate on independent timelines.

items.prompt: What does the client need to change when a route's entry is flipped from legacy to new?
choices: Nothing — the client never sees the routing table
The client's URL for that endpoint
The client's authentication token
The client's HTTP method for that route
items.explanation: The routing decision is invisible to the client by design — nothing on the client side needs to change.

items.prompt: If a route has no entry in the routing table at all, which system should serve it?
choices: Legacy, as the safe default
New, since it is assumed ready
Whichever system is under less load right now
The request should be rejected outright
items.explanation: Defaulting an unconfigured route to legacy avoids accidentally sending traffic to unproven code.

items.prompt: What is the smallest possible change needed to migrate exactly one route?
choices: Updating that one route's entry in the routing table
Rewriting the legacy system's handler for that route
Updating every other route's entry too, to stay consistent
Changing the DNS record for the whole domain
items.explanation: Because the table holds the decision per route, migrating one route is a single, isolated table update.

items.prompt: Between `GET /products` (read-only, high traffic) and `POST /orders` (writes money, lower traffic), which should typically migrate first?
choices: POST /orders, because it is the route that matters more to the business
GET /products — it is the cheapest way to prove the facade works, with a failure mode that is merely embarrassing rather than financially damaging
Whichever route happens to have the fewest lines of code behind it
They should always be migrated at exactly the same moment, together
items.explanation: Migration order should track blast radius, not business importance. A read-only route proves the facade and the new system's basics on real traffic without risking money if something goes wrong — earning confidence before tackling the riskier write path.
items.reflection: Ordering risky work by blast radius rather than by importance or convenience shows up well beyond migrations — it is why a surgeon operates on the lowest-stakes case first when learning a new technique, and why a pilot trains on calm weather before storms. Where have you seen (or made) the mistake of ordering work by importance instead of by how survivable a mistake would be?

items.prompt: A team migrates their dozen routes in alphabetical order. What is the problem with that?
choices: There is no problem at all — alphabetical order is as good as any other order
Alphabetical order has no relationship to risk or blast radius, so a high-stakes route can end up migrated before the facade has proven itself on safer traffic
Alphabetical order is technically disallowed under most engineering style guides
It only really works for the routes whose names start with letters A through M
items.explanation: Order should be chosen deliberately by risk, not by an arbitrary sort. Alphabetical order can just as easily put POST /orders before GET /products, migrating the highest-blast-radius route before the facade has any track record at all.
items.reflection: Ordering risky work by blast radius rather than by importance or convenience shows up well beyond migrations — it is why a surgeon operates on the lowest-stakes case first when learning a new technique, and why a pilot trains on calm weather before storms. Where have you seen (or made) the mistake of ordering work by importance instead of by how survivable a mistake would be?

items.prompt: A route is read-only but is called a thousand times more often than any write route. Does its high traffic volume make it riskier to migrate early?
choices: Not on its own — high traffic with no side effects is still a cheap failure mode; it is write access and the cost of being wrong that drive risk, not raw call count
Yes, any high-traffic route is automatically the riskiest route to migrate
Yes, because high traffic always means the new system will run out of resources
No, because read-only routes can never be migrated at all
items.explanation: Traffic volume affects how much evidence you gather quickly, not how expensive a failure is. A read-only route failing is embarrassing; a write route failing can be financially catastrophic regardless of how rarely it is called.
items.reflection: Ordering risky work by blast radius rather than by importance or convenience shows up well beyond migrations — it is why a surgeon operates on the lowest-stakes case first when learning a new technique, and why a pilot trains on calm weather before storms. Where have you seen (or made) the mistake of ordering work by importance instead of by how survivable a mistake would be?

items.prompt: A brand-new route, never seen in production before, is added at the same time the migration starts. Where should it land on the migration order, relative to existing read-only routes?
choices: After the facade has already earned confidence on existing read-only traffic — a never-proven route plus a never-proven facade is two unknowns stacked together
First, since new code is always the top priority
It does not matter, since it has no existing traffic to risk
It should skip the facade entirely and go straight to the new system
items.explanation: Stacking two unknowns (a brand-new route and an unproven facade) is riskier than letting the facade prove itself on known, safe traffic first, even though the new route technically has no prior traffic pattern to protect.
items.reflection: Ordering risky work by blast radius rather than by importance or convenience shows up well beyond migrations — it is why a surgeon operates on the lowest-stakes case first when learning a new technique, and why a pilot trains on calm weather before storms. Where have you seen (or made) the mistake of ordering work by importance instead of by how survivable a mistake would be?

items.prompt: Which signal should drive migration order?
choices: Risk and blast radius
Alphabetical order of the route name
The order routes were originally written in
Which developer happens to be free that week
items.explanation: Order should be chosen deliberately by how costly a mistake on that route would be.

items.prompt: Why is a read-only route usually a good first candidate to migrate?
choices: Its failure mode is cheap — nothing gets written incorrectly if it is wrong
It is always the most heavily used route
It requires no facade at all
It is guaranteed to have no bugs
items.explanation: A wrong read-only answer is embarrassing, not financially damaging — a cheap way to earn confidence.

items.prompt: Why is a route that writes money usually migrated later rather than earlier?
choices: Because a mistake on it can be financially costly and may need a compensating action
Because it is always technically harder to code
Because write routes cannot be shadowed under any circumstances
Because it is always called less often than read routes
items.explanation: The deciding factor is cost of failure, not technical difficulty.

items.prompt: Does migrating by risk mean the most business-critical route always goes first?
choices: No — business importance and migration-order risk are different things
Yes, the most important route for the business always goes first
Yes, but only on Mondays
Only if that route also happens to be the oldest one
items.explanation: A route can be very important to the business and also very risky to migrate early — those are separate axes.

items.prompt: What benefit does an early, low-risk migration give to every route migrated after it?
choices: A facade that has already been exercised at scale on real traffic
A free rewrite of the legacy system
Permission to skip the shadow stage entirely
Automatic retirement of the legacy code
items.explanation: Each successfully migrated route builds confidence in the facade itself, which benefits every subsequent migration.

items.prompt: What is wrong with choosing migration order purely by convenience (whichever route is easiest to code first)?
choices: It has no relationship to how costly a mistake on that route would be
Nothing is wrong with it — convenience is always the right ordering
It is technically impossible to migrate routes in that order
It only works for read-only routes
items.explanation: Convenience and risk are unrelated axes — an easy route to code can still be catastrophic to get wrong in production.

items.prompt: In the route lifecycle (legacy-only to shadow to migrated to retired), what distinguishes shadow from migrated?
choices: Nothing really distinguishes them — they are effectively the same underlying state, just given two different names
In shadow, the client still gets the legacy answer while the new system is only compared in the background; in migrated, the client's answer actually comes from the new system
Shadow specifically means the route has been fully disabled for every single visitor until further notice
Migrated specifically means the legacy code for that route has already been permanently deleted outright
items.explanation: Shadow is a zero-risk evidence-gathering stage — the client-visible answer never changes. Migrated is the point where the new system's answer actually reaches real users, which should only happen once shadow evidence supports it.
items.reflection: A staged lifecycle with a built-in way back is a more general idea than migrations — probation periods, feature-flag rollout stages, and canary releases all define the same kind of states-with-an-exit. Where have you seen a process that let you back out cleanly at an early stage, but not once it reached a later one?

items.prompt: A route sits in migrated for months, fully served by the new system, but its legacy code path is still deployed and untouched. Is that route retired?
choices: Yes — once traffic is fully on the new system, it is retired by definition
No — retirement is a separate, deliberate step (deleting the legacy code path), not something that happens automatically once traffic has moved
Yes, as long as that state has lasted for more than roughly a week
No — a route can technically never be retired while the legacy system exists at all
items.explanation: Migrated and retired are distinct states on purpose. A route can be fully migrated in traffic while its legacy implementation stays around as an untested rollback target — deleting that legacy code is a deliberate call made once enough migrated time has passed.
items.reflection: A staged lifecycle with a built-in way back is a more general idea than migrations — probation periods, feature-flag rollout stages, and canary releases all define the same kind of states-with-an-exit. Where have you seen a process that let you back out cleanly at an early stage, but not once it reached a later one?

items.prompt: A regression is found on a migrated route. According to the lifecycle, what is the valid next state?
choices: Retired — deleting the legacy code is the fix
Legacy-only — flip the route back until the regression is fixed
Shadow — the route must restart the entire evidence-gathering process from zero
The lifecycle has no path backward once a route is migrated
items.explanation: The lifecycle explicitly allows migrated to legacy-only as a direct move, which is exactly the fast rollback the facade is built for — no need to restart the full shadow evidence-gathering process for a route that had already proven itself before this regression.
items.reflection: A staged lifecycle with a built-in way back is a more general idea than migrations — probation periods, feature-flag rollout stages, and canary releases all define the same kind of states-with-an-exit. Where have you seen a process that let you back out cleanly at an early stage, but not once it reached a later one?

items.prompt: List the four states a route passes through, in order.
choices: Legacy-only, shadow, migrated, retired
Shadow, migrated, legacy-only, retired
Migrated, shadow, retired, legacy-only
Retired, migrated, shadow, legacy-only
items.explanation: This is the order a route earns its way through the lifecycle, from untouched legacy to fully retired.

items.prompt: In which state does the client's visible answer first start coming from the new system?
choices: Migrated
Shadow
Legacy-only
Retired
items.explanation: In shadow the client still gets the legacy answer; only in migrated does the new system's answer actually reach the client.

items.prompt: Can a route move directly from migrated back to legacy-only?
choices: Yes — that is the fast rollback the facade exists to support
No — a route can never move backward once migrated
Only by restarting the entire shadow stage first
Only if the legacy code has already been deleted
items.explanation: A direct migrated-to-legacy-only move is an explicit, valid path in the lifecycle — the whole point of keeping legacy around.

items.prompt: What must be true before a route leaves the retired state?
choices: Nothing — retired is the end of the lifecycle, there is no next state
It must restart from legacy-only automatically
It must go back to shadow first
It becomes migrated again after exactly one year
items.explanation: Retired is the terminal state in the lifecycle — the legacy code is gone, and there is nothing further to transition to.

items.prompt: What has to happen before a route can move from shadow to migrated?
choices: The new system's responses must consistently match the legacy system's
A fixed number of calendar days must pass, regardless of evidence
The legacy system's code must already be deleted
The route must be flagged as business-critical
items.explanation: The lifecycle gates the shadow-to-migrated move on evidence (consistent matching), not on a calendar or on importance.

items.prompt: Is migrated the same thing as retired?
choices: No — migrated means traffic moved; retired means the legacy code was also deleted
Yes, they describe the exact same state
Yes, but only for read-only routes
No — retired always comes before migrated
items.explanation: These are deliberately separate states: moving traffic and deleting the fallback are two different decisions.

items.prompt: At a high level, what does shadowing a route mean during a migration?
choices: Hiding a route from monitoring dashboards until it is fully migrated
Calling both the legacy and new system on real traffic, returning the legacy answer to the client, and recording whether the new system agreed
Copying the legacy system's entire database into the new system's storage
Running the new system only inside a staging environment, never on real traffic
items.explanation: Shadowing forwards real production traffic to the new system for comparison purposes only — the client always gets the legacy answer, so a bug in the unproven new system can never reach a real user during this stage.
items.reflection: Shadowing is really a general technique for de-risking a replacement before it has authority — a dry run that uses real conditions but withholds real consequences. Where have you seen a dry run or shadow process used outside software, like a trial run of a new policy alongside the old one before it actually takes effect?

items.prompt: During shadowing, the new system throws an error on a request the legacy system handled fine. What should happen from the client's point of view?
choices: The client sees the error directly, since it is genuine feedback about the new system
Nothing changes for the client — they still get the legacy system's answer, and the error is just logged as a mismatch
The request should fail entirely, since one of the two systems threw an error
The client should be shown both answers side by side and asked to pick one
items.explanation: Shadowing exists precisely so the new system's failures stay invisible to real users while still being captured as data. The client only ever sees the legacy system's answer during this stage.
items.reflection: Shadowing is really a general technique for de-risking a replacement before it has authority — a dry run that uses real conditions but withholds real consequences. Where have you seen a dry run or shadow process used outside software, like a trial run of a new policy alongside the old one before it actually takes effect?

items.prompt: Why does the facade return the legacy response during shadowing instead of the new system's response, given both are already computed?
choices: Because computing the new system's response during shadowing is only meant for logging purposes, and returning it would require writing a meaningful amount of extra code
Because shadowing's purpose is gathering evidence before any customer depends on the new system — returning its answer would make a bug in it a real incident instead of a logged comparison
Because the legacy system is, in nearly every real deployment, always meaningfully faster to respond than the brand-new one
There is no real reason behind that choice at all — either response would work equally well for this purpose
items.explanation: Returning the legacy answer keeps the blast radius at zero during the evidence-gathering stage. The moment the new system's answer reaches a real client, an undiscovered bug stops being a comparison-log entry and becomes an actual incident.
items.reflection: Shadowing is really a general technique for de-risking a replacement before it has authority — a dry run that uses real conditions but withholds real consequences. Where have you seen a dry run or shadow process used outside software, like a trial run of a new policy alongside the old one before it actually takes effect?

items.prompt: A route's shadow match rate has been 100% for two weeks. Is that alone sufficient reason to flip it fully to the new system?
choices: Yes — 100% agreement over two weeks means the new system has been fully proven
Not by itself — it only proves agreement on the traffic that actually occurred; low-frequency inputs or unusual data the shadow period never saw are still unproven
No — shadowing can never justify a flip at all, regardless of the match rate seen
Yes, but only if that particular match rate happened to be measured on a Friday
items.explanation: A high match rate over representative traffic is strong evidence, but it is still bounded by what traffic actually occurred during the window — it says nothing about paths that traffic hasn't exercised yet. The flip decision weighs that evidence against how costly an undiscovered gap would be for that specific route.
items.reflection: Shadowing is really a general technique for de-risking a replacement before it has authority — a dry run that uses real conditions but withholds real consequences. Where have you seen a dry run or shadow process used outside software, like a trial run of a new policy alongside the old one before it actually takes effect?

items.prompt: During shadowing, which system's answer does the real client actually receive?
choices: The legacy system's answer
The new system's answer
Whichever answer arrives first
Both answers, shown together
items.explanation: The client always gets the legacy answer during shadowing — the new system's answer is only compared, never shown.

items.prompt: What gets recorded when the new system's answer disagrees with the legacy system's during shadowing?
choices: A mismatch, logged for the team to review
Nothing — mismatches are discarded automatically
An automatic rollback of the whole route
An automatic flip of the route to new
items.explanation: Disagreements are logged as evidence, not acted on automatically — a human decides what to do with that evidence.

items.prompt: Is shadowing something a customer can notice happening?
choices: No — it is invisible to the customer by design
Yes, customers see a banner during shadowing
Yes, the page loads twice as slowly and this is expected
Only customers on a waitlist can notice it
items.explanation: Shadowing is specifically designed to be invisible — the whole point is zero customer-facing risk.

items.prompt: What kind of evidence does shadowing generate that a test suite alone cannot?
choices: Agreement (or disagreement) checked against real, unfiltered production traffic
A formal mathematical proof of correctness
A faster deployment pipeline
A smaller legacy codebase
items.explanation: Test suites only cover cases someone thought to write; shadowing is checked against whatever traffic production actually sends.

items.prompt: Does shadowing require the new system to be fully trusted already?
choices: No — shadowing is specifically for systems not yet trusted
Yes, only fully trusted systems can be shadowed
Yes, but only on weekends
Shadowing is only for the legacy system, never the new one
items.explanation: Shadowing exists exactly because the new system is not yet trusted — it is how that trust gets earned safely.

items.prompt: What is the main value of a single, isolated mismatch found during shadowing?
choices: It is a concrete, replayable bug report generated for free by real traffic
It automatically fixes itself over time
It proves the new system should never be trusted
It has no value unless it happens more than a hundred times
items.explanation: Every mismatch is a specific, investigable piece of evidence about a real gap between the two systems.

items.prompt: Why is retiring (deleting) the legacy code path treated as a separate, deliberate step rather than something that happens automatically at 100% migrated traffic?
choices: It genuinely isn't treated as a separate step in practice — retirement should happen the instant a route first hits 100% new traffic
Because the legacy path still serves as a tested-in-production rollback target, and deleting it too early removes that safety net before enough migrated time has proven the new system stable
Because legacy code, once written, can technically never actually be deleted from a running system, only disabled
Because deleting any piece of legacy code always requires going through an entirely separate full system rewrite
items.explanation: Keeping the legacy path around after a flip preserves the ability to roll back cheaply. Retirement gives that up in exchange for not maintaining dead code forever — a trade worth making only once enough time has passed to trust the new system without it.
items.reflection: Deciding when a safety net is no longer earning its keep is a trade-off that outlives this specific pattern — keeping an old backup process, an emergency contact, or a deprecated tool around 'just in case' costs something to maintain, and at some point the cost outweighs the comfort. How do you personally decide when a safety net has stopped earning its keep?

items.prompt: What happens if a team never retires any legacy code paths, even years after every route shows new in the routing table?
choices: Nothing bad happens at all in that scenario — it is strictly safer, in every respect, to just keep the old code forever
It defeats the purpose of migrating at all — it just relocates the does-anyone-still-understand-this problem instead of resolving it, while paying to maintain two systems indefinitely
The routing facade itself will eventually just stop working on its own, entirely unprompted by anyone
The legacy system will automatically and silently delete itself after some fixed, predetermined period of time
items.explanation: The whole point of the migration was to retire the legacy system's maintenance burden, not just stop sending it traffic. Never retiring anything keeps paying that cost indefinitely while gaining none of the simplification the migration was meant to deliver.
items.reflection: Deciding when a safety net is no longer earning its keep is a trade-off that outlives this specific pattern — keeping an old backup process, an emergency contact, or a deprecated tool around 'just in case' costs something to maintain, and at some point the cost outweighs the comfort. How do you personally decide when a safety net has stopped earning its keep?

items.prompt: What is a reasonable trigger for finally deleting a route's legacy code path?
choices: The very moment its routing table entry first shows new for that route
After enough migrated time has passed that a regression would rather be fixed forward than rolled back to code nobody has touched in months
Exactly one calendar year after the overall migration project started, every time
Only once every single route in the entire system has finished migrating
items.explanation: The right trigger is confidence-based, not calendar-based or all-or-nothing: once enough time and evidence has accumulated that reverting to stale, unmaintained legacy code is no longer the preferred fix for a regression, that route's legacy path can be safely deleted independent of other routes.
items.reflection: Deciding when a safety net is no longer earning its keep is a trade-off that outlives this specific pattern — keeping an old backup process, an emergency contact, or a deprecated tool around 'just in case' costs something to maintain, and at some point the cost outweighs the comfort. How do you personally decide when a safety net has stopped earning its keep?

items.prompt: What does retiring a route actually mean?
choices: Deleting its legacy code path
Flipping its routing table entry to new
Starting its shadow stage
Logging its first mismatch
items.explanation: Retirement is specifically the deletion of the old code, a separate step from moving traffic.

items.prompt: Is a route retired the instant it reaches 100% traffic on the new system?
choices: No — retirement is a separate, deliberate step taken later
Yes, always, automatically
Yes, but only for read-only routes
No — a route can never be retired
items.explanation: 100% new traffic means migrated, not retired — those are two different states.

items.prompt: What does the legacy code path provide while a route is migrated but not yet retired?
choices: A tested rollback target in case of regression
Faster response times than the new system
Additional new features
Nothing of value — it should be deleted immediately
items.explanation: The legacy path's remaining value after migration is purely as a cheap, proven fallback.

items.prompt: What is lost if a team never retires any legacy code, forever?
choices: The simplification benefit the migration was meant to deliver
Nothing — keeping everything is always strictly better
The ability to serve any traffic at all
The new system stops working
items.explanation: Maintaining both systems indefinitely means paying the old system's maintenance cost forever without ever gaining the simplification the migration was for.

items.prompt: Should every route in a migration be retired at the exact same time?
choices: No — each route can be retired independently once it has earned it
Yes, always, all at once
Yes, but only in alphabetical order
No, retirement must happen before migration
items.explanation: Retirement is decided per route, based on that route's own accumulated confidence, not on a single shared deadline.

items.prompt: What is a sensible basis for deciding a route is ready to retire?
choices: Enough migrated time has passed that rolling back to stale legacy code is no longer the preferred fix
A fixed number of calendar days, the same for every route regardless of risk
Whether the legacy code still compiles
Whether the original author of the legacy code still works at the company
items.explanation: Confidence, not a fixed calendar rule, is what should trigger retirement.

items.prompt: Implement `stableBucket(identity)` so it returns a deterministic integer between 0 and 99 for a given identity string. The same identity must always produce the same bucket — no `Math.random()` involved.

tests.description: same identity gives same bucket every call
different identities can give different buckets

items.explanation: A deterministic string hash (multiply-and-add over character codes, folded into a 32-bit int with `| 0`) followed by `% 100` gives a stable bucket with no external state and no per-call randomness — the same identity always lands in the same bucket, which is exactly what a rollout that shouldn't flip mid-session needs.
items.reflection: Trading precise, hand-picked control for a stable, repeatable computation with zero storage overhead is a trade-off bigger than rollouts — hashing shows up anywhere something needs a consistent, shardable assignment without a lookup table (consistent hashing in caches, partition assignment in distributed databases). Where else have you seen a system prefer a deterministic computation over a stored decision, to avoid the cost of storing and looking it up?

items.prompt: Implement `stableBucket(key)` returning a deterministic 0-99 integer for a string key, such that `stableBucket('a:x')` and `stableBucket('b:x')` are allowed to differ even though both contain 'x' — the whole key matters, not just part of it.

tests.description: full key matters, not a substring

items.explanation: Hashing over every character of the full key (not a substring) means two keys that merely share a fragment, like both ending in ':x', still hash independently based on their complete content — this is what lets a route+identity composite key give each route its own independent bucket assignment for the same identity.
items.reflection: Trading precise, hand-picked control for a stable, repeatable computation with zero storage overhead is a trade-off bigger than rollouts — hashing shows up anywhere something needs a consistent, shardable assignment without a lookup table (consistent hashing in caches, partition assignment in distributed databases). Where else have you seen a system prefer a deterministic computation over a stored decision, to avoid the cost of storing and looking it up?

items.prompt: Implement `bucketsAgree(hashFn, key1, key2)` returning true if `hashFn(key1) === hashFn(key2)`. This is the edge case: a correct deterministic hash function can still have two unrelated keys collide into the same bucket by pure chance. Write the comparison helper, not a new hash.

tests.description: works with the real stableBucket-style hash too
tests.expr: const h = (k) => { let hash=0; for (let i=0;i<k.length;i++) hash=(hash*31+k.charCodeAt(i))|0; return Math.abs(hash)%100; }; expect(bucketsAgree(h, 'user-1', 'user-1')).toBeTruthy()

items.explanation: A collision between two unrelated keys landing in the same bucket is expected probabilistically (about a 1% chance per pair with 100 buckets) and is not itself a bug — it just means those two unrelated identities happen to share a rollout bucket for this stage, not that the hash function is broken. Detecting a collision is a simple equality check once both sides are hashed.
items.reflection: Trading precise, hand-picked control for a stable, repeatable computation with zero storage overhead is a trade-off bigger than rollouts — hashing shows up anywhere something needs a consistent, shardable assignment without a lookup table (consistent hashing in caches, partition assignment in distributed databases). Where else have you seen a system prefer a deterministic computation over a stored decision, to avoid the cost of storing and looking it up?

items.prompt: Implement `isInRange(bucket)` returning true if `bucket` is an integer between 0 and 99 inclusive.
items.explanation: A valid bucket is always within [0, 99] — this is the basic contract any stable-bucket implementation must honor.

items.prompt: Implement `toBucket(hash)` which turns a raw (possibly negative) integer hash into a 0-99 bucket using `Math.abs` and modulo.

tests.description: negative hash still lands in range

items.explanation: Taking the absolute value before the modulo is what keeps a negative raw hash (a normal outcome of integer overflow in a hash function) inside the valid 0-99 range.

items.prompt: Implement `isDeterministic(fn, input)` which calls `fn(input)` twice and returns whether both calls produced the exact same result.

tests.description: a random function is not deterministic

items.explanation: Determinism means calling the same function with the same input twice gives the same answer — this is the exact property that distinguishes a stable bucket hash from a per-request coin flip.

items.prompt: Implement `combineKey(path, identity)` returning a single string that joins `path` and `identity` with a colon, e.g. `combineKey('GET /products', 'user-1')` returns `'GET /products:user-1'`.

tests.description: joins path and identity with a colon
different identities give different combined keys

items.explanation: Combining the route and the identity into one key before hashing is what gives each route its own independent bucket assignment for the same identity, instead of one bucket shared across every route.

items.prompt: Implement `percentOfBuckets(percent)` returning how many of the 100 buckets (0-99) fall under a given rollout percentage. For example, `percentOfBuckets(5)` returns `5`.
items.explanation: With exactly 100 buckets, the rollout percentage and the bucket count under that percentage are the same number by construction — that 1-to-1 mapping is why 100 buckets was chosen in the first place.

items.prompt: Given a `stableBucket(key)` function (already implemented, deterministic 0-99) and a route's `rolloutPercent` (0-100), implement `resolveTarget(bucket, rolloutPercent)` returning 'new' if the bucket falls under the rollout percentage, else 'legacy'. Treat `rolloutPercent <= 0` as always legacy and `>= 100` as always new.

tests.description: bucket under the percent is new
bucket at or above the percent is legacy

items.explanation: Comparing the identity's fixed bucket against the current rollout percentage gives a stable, gradually-widening slice of identities landing on 'new' as the percentage increases over time, while any single identity's answer never flips back and forth as long as the percentage itself doesn't change.
items.reflection: A pure decision function with no I/O and no shared state is easy to trust precisely because its output depends on nothing but its inputs — that same discipline (push decisions into small, pure, boring functions; push side effects to the edges) is a general design habit, not a strangler-fig-specific one. Where have you kept a risky decision in a small pure function on purpose, separate from the messier code that calls it?

items.prompt: Implement `resolveTarget(config, bucket)` where `config` is `{ target: 'legacy' | 'new', rolloutPercent?: number }`. If `config.target === 'legacy'`, always return 'legacy' regardless of rollout. Otherwise apply the rollout percentage against `bucket` the same way as a normal gradual rollout (undefined percent means fully 'new').

tests.description: target new with no rolloutPercent is fully new
target new with rolloutPercent respects the bucket

items.explanation: The route's own `target` field is checked first as a hard override — a route explicitly marked legacy should never be pulled toward 'new' by a stale rollout percentage left over from an earlier configuration. Only once `target === 'new'` does the percentage-based bucket comparison apply at all.
items.reflection: A pure decision function with no I/O and no shared state is easy to trust precisely because its output depends on nothing but its inputs — that same discipline (push decisions into small, pure, boring functions; push side effects to the edges) is a general design habit, not a strangler-fig-specific one. Where have you kept a risky decision in a small pure function on purpose, separate from the messier code that calls it?

items.prompt: A route's `rolloutPercent` is accidentally set to a negative number (a bad config push, e.g. -10). Implement `resolveTarget(bucket, rolloutPercent)` so this edge case still fails safe to 'legacy', the same as a percent of exactly 0 would.

tests.description: negative percent fails safe to legacy

items.explanation: Using `<= 0` rather than `=== 0` as the legacy boundary means a malformed negative value (from a bad config push, not just a deliberate 0) still fails safe to legacy instead of accidentally falling through to the comparison branch and behaving unpredictably.
items.reflection: A pure decision function with no I/O and no shared state is easy to trust precisely because its output depends on nothing but its inputs — that same discipline (push decisions into small, pure, boring functions; push side effects to the edges) is a general design habit, not a strangler-fig-specific one. Where have you kept a risky decision in a small pure function on purpose, separate from the messier code that calls it?

items.prompt: Implement `isFullRollout(percent)` returning true if `percent` is 100 or more.
items.explanation: 100% (or anything at or above it) means every bucket is included — a full rollout to 'new'.

items.prompt: Implement `isNoRollout(percent)` returning true if `percent` is 0 or less.
items.explanation: 0% or less means no bucket qualifies — this is the always-legacy edge of the rollout.

items.prompt: Implement `inRolloutWindow(bucket, percent)` returning true if `bucket < percent`, with no edge-case handling needed.

tests.description: bucket below percent is in window
bucket equal to percent is not in window
bucket above percent is not in window

items.explanation: This strict less-than comparison is the core piece that `resolveTarget` builds on once the 0 and 100 edge cases are handled separately.

items.prompt: Implement `targetLabel(isNew)` returning the string 'new' if `isNew` is true, otherwise 'legacy'.
items.explanation: This is the final mapping step from a boolean decision to the label the rest of the system actually consumes.

items.prompt: Implement `clampPercent(p)` that clamps a number into the range [0, 100] — values below 0 become 0, values above 100 become 100, and values in between are unchanged.
items.explanation: Clamping before storing or using a rollout percentage is a cheap way to make a malformed config value harmless instead of letting it propagate into resolveTarget's branches unchecked.

items.prompt: A route's shadow log has zero entries so far — no traffic has hit it yet. What should its match rate read as, and why?
choices: 1 (100%) — an empty log is not evidence of disagreement, so defaulting to a misleading 0% would wrongly suggest the new system has already failed
0 (0%) — no evidence should always be treated as the worst case
It should throw an error, since dividing zero matches by zero entries is undefined
It should be left blank until the first request arrives
items.explanation: Defaulting an empty log to a 100% match rate avoids a misleading 0/0 reading and correctly reflects that no evidence yet is not the same claim as proven to disagree.
items.reflection: Choosing what an absence of evidence should mean (innocent until shown otherwise, not guilty by default) is a judgment call bigger than this one metric — the same question comes up in test coverage reports, uptime dashboards, and even legal reasoning. Where have you seen a system treat silence or absence of data as bad news, when it should have treated it as simply unknown?

items.prompt: A unit's overall match rate across all routes sits at a healthy 98%. One specific route, `POST /cart`, is actually at 40% underneath that average, but it only makes up 2% of total shadow traffic. What does the overall number hide?
choices: Nothing — the overall average is always the number that matters most for a decision
A route-specific failure can be diluted into invisibility by an aggregate average across all routes, so match rate needs to be computed per route, not just overall
The overall average can never be computed correctly unless every route has equal traffic
98% overall always implies every individual route is also near 98%
items.explanation: A single blended average can hide a badly broken low-traffic route behind many healthy high-traffic ones — match rate has to be computed per route (or per path) to be actionable, exactly the mismatch that `POST /cart` here would otherwise sail through unnoticed.
items.reflection: Choosing what an absence of evidence should mean (innocent until shown otherwise, not guilty by default) is a judgment call bigger than this one metric — the same question comes up in test coverage reports, uptime dashboards, and even legal reasoning. Where have you seen a system treat silence or absence of data as bad news, when it should have treated it as simply unknown?

items.prompt: Why is a logged list of individual mismatches more useful to an engineer investigating a problem than the match-rate percentage alone?
choices: The percentage alone says something is wrong but not what; the individual mismatches are concrete, replayable examples a team can actually debug
The percentage is always wrong and should be ignored entirely
Individual mismatches are only useful for billing purposes, not debugging
There is no real difference — both convey exactly the same information
items.explanation: A rate is a summary; the mismatches list is the raw evidence behind that summary, specific enough to actually investigate and fix.
items.reflection: Choosing what an absence of evidence should mean (innocent until shown otherwise, not guilty by default) is a judgment call bigger than this one metric — the same question comes up in test coverage reports, uptime dashboards, and even legal reasoning. Where have you seen a system treat silence or absence of data as bad news, when it should have treated it as simply unknown?

items.prompt: The new system's answer for a shadowed request is arguably more correct than the legacy system's (e.g. a trimmed string versus one with trailing whitespace), but the two still don't match byte-for-byte. Should this count as a mismatch in the shadow log?
choices: Yes — the log should record the literal disagreement regardless of which side seems more correct; the team decides afterward whether it is an acceptable diff or a bug to fix
No — if the new system is more correct, the log should automatically mark it as matched
No — mismatches should only be logged for crashes, never for value differences
Yes, but only if the difference is larger than one character
items.explanation: The log's job is to report facts (did the two answers agree), not to make a judgment call about which one is better — that judgment belongs to the team reviewing the evidence, since a downstream caller doing an exact comparison won't care which side was 'more correct.'
items.reflection: Choosing what an absence of evidence should mean (innocent until shown otherwise, not guilty by default) is a judgment call bigger than this one metric — the same question comes up in test coverage reports, uptime dashboards, and even legal reasoning. Where have you seen a system treat silence or absence of data as bad news, when it should have treated it as simply unknown?

items.prompt: What does a shadow log's match rate represent?
choices: The fraction of shadowed calls where the new system agreed with the legacy system
The percentage of total traffic that has been migrated to new
How fast the new system responds compared to legacy
The number of routes currently in the shadow state
items.explanation: Match rate is purely about agreement between the two systems' answers, not about speed or migration progress.

items.prompt: What is a mismatch in a shadow log?
choices: A recorded case where the new system's answer disagreed with the legacy system's
A request that failed to reach either system
A route that has never been shadowed
A difference in which HTTP method was used
items.explanation: A mismatch is specifically a disagreement in answers between the two systems on the same request.

items.prompt: Does a high overall match rate across an entire unit guarantee every individual route is healthy?
choices: No — an average can hide one badly broken low-traffic route
Yes, a high average always means every route is fine
Yes, but only if there are fewer than five routes total
No, because match rate cannot be averaged at all
items.explanation: Aggregates can dilute a specific route's problem — match rate should also be checked per route.

items.prompt: Why is a logged mismatch described as a 'free' bug report?
choices: Because it was generated by real traffic that would have happened anyway, with no extra test-writing effort
Because finding it costs nothing in engineering time to investigate
Because the new system automatically fixes itself once a mismatch is found
Because it is always a false positive
items.explanation: The traffic that produced the mismatch was already happening — shadowing just captures evidence from it that a hand-written test suite might never have thought to cover.

items.prompt: What should a shadow-log function return for an empty log with no entries yet?
choices: A match rate of 1 (100%), since there is no evidence of disagreement
A match rate of 0, treating no evidence as the worst case
An error, since it cannot be computed
Undefined, with no defined behavior
items.explanation: Defaulting to 100% avoids a misleading 0/0 and correctly represents 'no evidence of a problem yet.'

items.prompt: Is agreeing with legacy on a test suite the same bar as agreeing with legacy in a shadow log?
choices: No — the shadow log checks against real, unfiltered production traffic, a stricter and more honest bar
Yes, they are exactly the same bar
No, the shadow log is always an easier bar to pass
Yes, but only for read-only routes
items.explanation: A test suite only covers what someone thought to test; shadowing is judged against whatever traffic production actually sends.

items.prompt: A route has never been explicitly set in the routing table. What should the lookup return for it, and why does that choice matter?
choices: 'legacy' — a brand-new or forgotten route is automatically safe by default, never accidentally served by unproven code just because nobody configured it
'new' — defaulting to the newest system is always the better assumption
Whichever system is currently handling more traffic overall
It should throw an error rather than returning any default
items.explanation: Defaulting an unset route to 'legacy' means a route nobody has explicitly migrated can never silently land on unproven new code — safety comes from the default itself, not from someone remembering to configure every route.
items.reflection: Choosing a safe default for the unconfigured case is a general defensive habit — permission systems default to deny, not allow; parsers default to rejecting unrecognized input, not guessing at it. Where have you seen a system get this backwards, defaulting to the risky choice instead of the safe one when nothing was explicitly configured?

items.prompt: A routing lookup is written to treat any truthy value for a route's target as meaning 'serve from new', instead of checking for the exact string 'new'. What bug does this risk?
choices: A typo, an unexpected value, or even the string 'legacy' itself (which is truthy) could all be misread as meaning new, silently routing traffic to unproven code
No real risk — truthy checks and exact-string checks always behave identically here
It would cause every request to fail outright
It only matters for numeric route configurations, never for strings
items.explanation: Checking for the exact string 'new' rather than any truthy value avoids a subtle class of bugs where a typo, an unexpected value, or even a non-empty 'legacy' string could be misread as a signal to route to the new system.
items.reflection: Choosing a safe default for the unconfigured case is a general defensive habit — permission systems default to deny, not allow; parsers default to rejecting unrecognized input, not guessing at it. Where have you seen a system get this backwards, defaulting to the risky choice instead of the safe one when nothing was explicitly configured?

items.prompt: A config push accidentally sets a route's target field to the typo'd value `'NEW'` (capitalized) instead of `'new'`. With a strict exact-match check against `'new'`, what happens to that route's traffic?
choices: It falls through to the safe default and keeps serving from legacy, since 'NEW' does not exactly match 'new'
It immediately serves 100% of traffic from the new system, because the intent was obviously 'new'
It crashes the facade entirely
It is split 50/50 between legacy and new
items.explanation: A strict, case-sensitive match against the expected value means a typo like 'NEW' simply fails to match and falls through to the safe default (legacy) — exactly the fail-safe behavior a config mistake should trigger, rather than silently being 'close enough' to count as new.
items.reflection: Choosing a safe default for the unconfigured case is a general defensive habit — permission systems default to deny, not allow; parsers default to rejecting unrecognized input, not guessing at it. Where have you seen a system get this backwards, defaulting to the risky choice instead of the safe one when nothing was explicitly configured?

items.prompt: What should an unconfigured route default to?
choices: Legacy
New
Whichever system responded most recently to any request
A random choice each time
items.explanation: Legacy is the safe default — a route nobody configured should never accidentally run unproven code.

items.prompt: Why check for the exact string 'new' instead of any truthy value when deciding a route's target?
choices: To avoid a typo or stray value being misread as meaning new
Because truthy checks are always slower to execute
Because JavaScript cannot compare strings exactly
There is no real reason, both checks are equivalent
items.explanation: An exact-match check treats anything other than the precise expected value as not-new, which fails safe toward legacy.

items.prompt: A newly added route is deployed to production before anyone has configured its routing entry. What happens to its traffic?
choices: It is served by legacy, by default
It is served by new, by default
It is rejected outright
It is served by whichever backend is listed first alphabetically
items.explanation: The safe-default behavior applies the same way to a brand-new route as to any other unconfigured one.

items.prompt: What is the main benefit of 'safety by default' in a routing table lookup?
choices: A missing or malformed configuration cannot accidentally send traffic to unproven code
It makes the new system respond faster
It removes the need for a facade entirely
It guarantees 100% match rate on shadowed routes
items.explanation: The point of a safe default is specifically to make missing or bad configuration harmless rather than risky.

items.prompt: If a routing config value is `undefined` for a given route, is that the same situation as it being explicitly set to 'legacy'?
choices: Functionally yes — both should result in the route being served by legacy
No, undefined should always cause an error
No, undefined should always mean new
They cannot be compared at all
items.explanation: Whether a route is unset or explicitly flagged legacy, the safe behavior is the same: serve from legacy.

items.prompt: Which of these config values should fail safe to legacy under a strict exact-match check against 'new'?
choices: The string 'NEW' (wrong case)
The exact string 'new'
Both values should resolve to new
Neither value matters, since routes never fail safe
items.explanation: A strict, case-sensitive match only accepts the exact expected string — any variation, including a case mismatch, falls through to the safe default.

items.prompt: Why can `GET` and `HEAD` requests be shadowed against the new system 'for free', but `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and `PATCH` cannot?
choices: Because read-only methods have no side effects to duplicate, while calling a mutating method on the new system for real would actually create a second real-world effect
Because GET and HEAD requests are always faster to process than the others
Because mutating methods are not allowed to be sent over HTTPS
There is no real difference; all methods can be shadowed identically
items.explanation: Shadowing calls both systems for comparison. For a read, that costs nothing extra. For a write, actually calling the new system's write path would duplicate the side effect (e.g. create a second real order), so mutating routes need a different verification strategy than plain shadowing.
items.reflection: Separating what is safe to do twice from what is not is a distinction bigger than HTTP methods — it is why dry-run modes exist for scripts that delete files, and why 'check' commands are kept separate from 'apply' commands in infrastructure tools. Where have you seen a system (or a habit of your own) carefully separate a safe-to-repeat check from an action that cannot be undone?

items.prompt: A `POST /orders` route is flipped back to legacy after a regression is found on the new system, but the new system had already charged a customer's card for one order before the flip happened. Does flipping the route back undo that charge?
choices: No — rolling back the route only affects where the *next* request goes; it does nothing to reverse an effect a *previous* request already caused on the new system
Yes — flipping the routing table entry automatically reverses any side effect the new system already caused
Yes, but only if the flip happens within 60 seconds of the original charge
No, because POST routes can never be rolled back under any circumstances
items.explanation: Routing is about where future requests go, not about undoing what already happened. A charge that already occurred on the new system needs its own compensating action (a refund, a cancellation) — the routing flip alone cannot touch it.
items.reflection: Separating what is safe to do twice from what is not is a distinction bigger than HTTP methods — it is why dry-run modes exist for scripts that delete files, and why 'check' commands are kept separate from 'apply' commands in infrastructure tools. Where have you seen a system (or a habit of your own) carefully separate a safe-to-repeat check from an action that cannot be undone?

items.prompt: A team wants evidence that their new `POST /orders` implementation is correct before trusting it with real traffic, but they cannot shadow it the normal way without creating duplicate orders. Which strategy fits the constraint?
choices: Verify it against a sandboxed copy of the new system (or dry-run logic that computes the result without committing it), rather than calling the real write path twice
Skip verification entirely and flip straight to 100% new traffic
Shadow it normally; duplicate orders are an acceptable cost of migration
Only ever migrate POST /orders by deleting the legacy system first
items.explanation: Since calling the real write path twice is not an option for a mutating route, verification has to happen against a sandbox or a dry-run path that produces a comparable result without a real side effect, or through a very small rollout percentage with fast rollback instead of shadowing.
items.reflection: Separating what is safe to do twice from what is not is a distinction bigger than HTTP methods — it is why dry-run modes exist for scripts that delete files, and why 'check' commands are kept separate from 'apply' commands in infrastructure tools. Where have you seen a system (or a habit of your own) carefully separate a safe-to-repeat check from an action that cannot be undone?

items.prompt: A `PATCH /profile` route (a mutating method) is being considered for migration. Does the general rule about GET/HEAD being safe to shadow apply to it?
choices: No — PATCH mutates state just like POST, PUT, and DELETE, so it carries the same duplicate-side-effect risk and needs the same non-shadowing strategy
Yes, PATCH is always treated as read-only by convention
It depends only on how long the PATCH request takes to process
PATCH is a special case that can always be safely shadowed, unlike POST
items.explanation: PATCH is a mutating method by convention, in the same family as POST, PUT, and DELETE — it carries the same risk of duplicating a real side effect if called twice for a naive shadow comparison.
items.reflection: Separating what is safe to do twice from what is not is a distinction bigger than HTTP methods — it is why dry-run modes exist for scripts that delete files, and why 'check' commands are kept separate from 'apply' commands in infrastructure tools. Where have you seen a system (or a habit of your own) carefully separate a safe-to-repeat check from an action that cannot be undone?

items.prompt: Which HTTP methods are safe to shadow against the new system for free?
choices: GET and HEAD
POST and DELETE
PUT and PATCH
All methods, equally
items.explanation: Only read-only methods have no side effect to duplicate when called a second time for comparison.

items.prompt: What goes wrong if you naively shadow a `POST /orders` route the same way as a `GET` route?
choices: It would create a second real order as a side effect of the comparison call
Nothing — POST routes shadow exactly the same as GET routes
The legacy system would stop responding
It would corrupt the routing table
items.explanation: Calling a real write path a second time for comparison duplicates its side effect — this is specific to mutating methods.

items.prompt: Does flipping a routing table entry back to legacy undo a write that the new system already performed?
choices: No — it only changes where future requests go
Yes, it automatically reverses any prior write
Yes, but only for orders under a certain dollar amount
It depends on which day of the week the flip happens
items.explanation: Routing table flips are forward-looking only; they cannot touch an effect that already happened.

items.prompt: What should be defined before a mutating route is migrated, not improvised during an incident?
choices: A compensating action, like a refund or cancellation
A new marketing page
A faster database index
A new client-side framework
items.explanation: A compensating action needs to exist ahead of time so a bad flip or regression has a real way to undo its effect.

items.prompt: Which category does `DELETE` fall into for shadowing purposes?
choices: Mutating — it needs a different verification strategy than plain shadowing
Read-only — it is always safe to shadow for free
Neither category applies to DELETE
It depends only on the response status code
items.explanation: DELETE changes state, so it belongs with POST, PUT, and PATCH as a mutating method that cannot be naively shadowed.

items.prompt: What is one alternative to naive shadowing for verifying a mutating route before trusting it?
choices: Verifying against a sandboxed copy of the new system, or using a small rollout percentage with fast rollback
Deleting the legacy system first, then seeing what happens
Running the migration only at night when traffic is low
Disabling the route entirely until the whole migration finishes
items.explanation: A sandbox (or dry-run) avoids the real side effect, and a small, closely watched rollout substitutes for shadowing when a true dry comparison isn't available.
